name: TwinSync guided demo -- KL CBD, six acts
note: Beats narrate the timeline already authored in scenario.json. Nothing here injects a fault or a storm: the scripted run is the source of truth, so the same keystroke gives the same demo every time. The chaos panel stays the manual override for questions asked off-script. Every figure quoted in a body below is read from the measured run rather than asserted.

beats.title: A city with a Z axis
beats.body: 2,074 OSM footprints, extruded to height, standing on a Copernicus GLO-30 elevation grid. 15 telecom sites, four field crews. Every tower runs a 3 KB ONNX anomaly model locally.
beats.say: This is Kuala Lumpur's CBD as our twin sees it — not a flat map, a city with height.

beats.title: Events, not telemetry
beats.body: The edge agents uplink state changes only. Watch the uplink tile: raw telemetry would be tens of megabytes; we send under a megabyte.
beats.say: Nothing is wrong yet. Notice what the network is not sending.

beats.title: A relay's backhaul saturates
beats.body: KL-03. EWMA and Mahalanobis flag it at full rate; the ONNX autoencoder confirms on its duty cycle. Detected 3.6 s after onset — before a single customer has called. The MTTD tile is live from here: 10.0 min reactive against seconds on the edge. KL-03 is a relay: KL-10, KL-12 and KL-13 all reach the network through it.
beats.say: Act one. The edge caught this in under four seconds — the detection tile is the whole argument in one number.

beats.title: But who actually lost service?
beats.body: Left: the flat coverage model dispatch uses today. Right: true line of sight, ray-cast against terrain and buildings at 60% Fresnel clearance. Same instant, same fault — read the verdict bar.
beats.say: Here is the whole argument. Same fault, two models of the world.

beats.title: Not a second fault — a chain reaction
beats.body: KL-13 alarms 148 s later, 301 m away. It is not a coincidence of geography: KL-03 is KL-13's primary feed, and every packet KL-13 sends transits it. ST-DBSCAN groups them into one incident — CL-001, 2 sites within 301 m over 148 s. Then the asset graph orders the cluster: who feeds whom, and who alarmed first. Both point the same way. SOURCE: KL-03. DOWNSTREAM: KL-13, one hop, on its primary feed. The amber link on the map is the direction the failure travelled.
beats.say: A second site alarms. It is not a second fault — it is the first one, arriving downstream. Watch the amber link: that is the direction the failure travelled.

beats.title: One truck roll, and the right end of it first
beats.body: CREW-C is already en route to KL-03, so KL-13 folds onto the same trip — a 1.7 minute detour instead of a second van. The second job waits, and the p90 still improves, 41.6 min to 29.3, because the baseline's ten-minute detection delay costs it more than the detour costs us. The crew works KL-03 first: KL-13 is downstream of it, so it clears when the head is fixed.
beats.say: One van covers both, and it starts at the end of the chain that actually needs fixing.

beats.title: A third fault — and it is unrelated
beats.body: KL-09 is 1,205 m from KL-03 and 1,015 m from KL-13 — both outside the 900 m radius — so ST-DBSCAN labels it ISOLATED rather than folding it into CL-001. It alarms 169 s after KL-13, well inside the ten-minute window, and carries the same fault type as KL-03 — and it still stays out, because distance is the only gate that separates them. No cluster means no head to name, so the incident card carries no source — this one is its own job. It commits the second of four vans.
beats.say: Act three. Same fault type as act one, a kilometre away — and the clustering keeps it separate. No cause named here, and a second van goes out.

beats.title: The monsoon arrives
beats.body: A convective cell enters from the north-east, 1.6 km across, tracking south-west over the CBD at 16 km/h. Right now it is barely registering — what matters is where it goes. It builds to 49 mm/hr by the time the roads start going under, 80 by the time the next site fails, and 95 at its peak. ITU-R P.838 rain fade is applied to the 18 GHz backhaul underneath it; the 2.1 GHz access carrier is unaffected at these rates, so nothing drops off the coverage map from weather alone. The weather tile turns amber and starts counting.
beats.say: And on top of it, the weather. A storm cell moves in — and it gets worse for the rest of the run.

beats.title: Elevation picks the crew's route
beats.body: The water is up. The DEM knows which road segments sit in the bottom decile of elevation; the storm knows where rain is falling right now; OSM knows which of those are on a crew's route. Where all three agree, the segment is repriced 3.2× in the travel-time graph, so A* stops treating it as a shortcut and routes the van around it. From here every dispatch decision — which crew, which road, which ETA — is solved on that graph instead of a flat map, which is why the nearest van stops being the fastest one.
beats.say: This is where elevation stops being scenery — it picks the crew's route, and A* drives round the water. Watch the cyan segments.

beats.title: Fourth site goes dark
beats.body: KL-06 loses mains and the fourth site goes dark: KL-03, then KL-13, then KL-09, now KL-06. No single one of these did the damage on its own — what matters is the total across all four, and this is the widest the gap gets. True line of sight says 47 buildings and 9,026 subscribers are off the air; the flat model says 3 buildings and 3 subscribers, missing 9,023 people — not by raising a false alarm, but by staying quiet. It holds only until KL-07 lands 95 s later.
beats.say: A fourth site goes dark. True line of sight says 47 buildings and 9,026 subscribers are off the air — the flat map says three.

beats.title: The last crew goes out
beats.body: KL-07 fails: a small fault on a distant site, 909 m from every other faulted tower, so it neither batches onto an in-flight trip nor joins a cluster. Five sites dark now — 49 buildings and 9,700 subscribers against the flat model's 3. It takes the last van, and the fleet is fully committed.
beats.say: A fifth site, and the last crew rolls. Every van is now out.

beats.title: The site nobody can ignore
beats.body: KL-04 loses power: 42,053 subscribers and two pieces of critical infrastructure behind it, and the incident it raises covers 53,399 subscribers across 134 buildings. Priority is reach × severity × criticality × urgency, and it scores 144.2 against 0.1 to 4.4 for everything already open. All four vans are committed, so this is the one moment the twin overrides a decision it has already made: it pulls CREW-C off KL-03. CREW-C is further away than CREW-D in metres but 8.6 min out against 13.1, so travel time beats distance.
beats.say: And now the one that changes the shape of the day. Watch a crew get pulled off its job.

beats.title: Six sites down, and the gap is significant
beats.body: All six down. True line of sight says 134 buildings and 53,399 subscribers; the flat model says 71. Even once the flat map finally notices something is wrong it is short by 25,381 people, and the two critical sites behind KL-04 are among the ones it never saw.
beats.say: The gap does not close as it gets worse — it widens. That is the case for building the twin with a Z axis.
